chapters.name: Chapter 1: Set up products that sell

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Researching a product niche
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a product niche and check that people are already buying.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI assistant and a real marketplace, you will choose a product niche and show evidence that people are already buying in it, with at least three real marketplace examples as evidence.
A niche is a specific group of buyers with a specific need: "handmade dog collars for large breeds", "natural hair-care kits for kids", "gardening tools for small balconies". Niches are easier to win than general categories.
Use AI to brainstorm: "I can make or source [products]. Suggest ten niches, the buyer for each, and what problem the product solves." Then check real demand yourself: search the marketplace for similar products, look at how many reviews top sellers have, read their 3-star reviews for complaints you could fix, and look at search suggestions.
AI cannot see live sales data reliably and may invent numbers. Use it for ideas and questions; use real marketplace pages and your own conversations for evidence.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for ten niche ideas based on what you can make or source.
- Search a marketplace for each top idea.
- Note top sellers' review counts and prices.
- Read 3-star reviews for problems you could fix.
- Pick one niche with clear demand.
Words to know:
- Niche: a specific group of buyers with a specific need.
- Demand: how many people want to buy something.
- Marketplace: a website where many sellers list products, like Etsy, Amazon or eBay.
Try it now: Use AI to brainstorm ten niches, check three of them on a real marketplace, and write a one-paragraph summary of the niche you choose with your evidence of demand.
You can now choose a product niche based on real evidence of demand.

check.q: What counts as evidence that people are already buying in a niche?
options: An AI tool saying the niche is popular
Real marketplace listings with sales and reviews
Your friends saying they like the idea
A niche with no sellers at all
check.why: Real listings with sales and reviews show actual demand, while AI can invent numbers.

check.q: You have ten niche ideas from AI. What would you do next?
options: Pick the one AI listed first
Start buying stock for all ten
Check a few of them on a real marketplace before choosing
Choose the one with the longest name
check.why: Checking ideas on a real marketplace turns AI brainstorming into evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing honest product listings
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a product title and description with AI that is clear, searchable and true.
This lesson builds toward: Given the real facts about a product, you will write a product listing with AI help that is clear, searchable and true, with every claim checked and nothing untrue left in.
A good listing answers the buyer's questions before they ask: what it is, who it is for, size, materials, what is included, care instructions and shipping time. The title should use the words buyers search for, without stuffing in keywords.
Give AI the real facts and ask: "Write a product title under 80 characters and a description with a short intro, 5 bullet points and care instructions. Use only these facts: [facts]." AI often adds features you did not mention; delete anything that is not true.
The FTC says ads must be truthful and backed by evidence. Do not claim "organic", "handmade", "made in USA", health benefits or "best seller" unless it is true and you can prove it. Check each platform's own listing rules too.
Step by step:
- Write down every real fact about the product.
- Ask AI for a title and description using only those facts.
- Delete anything AI added that is not true.
- Check claims like organic, handmade or made in USA.
- Check the platform's listing rules.
Words to know:
- Listing: a product's page on a store or marketplace.
- Keyword: a word or phrase buyers type into search.
Official sources:
- FTC: Advertising and Marketing Basics
Try it now: Write the facts for three products and use AI to draft each listing. Remove anything untrue and check every claim.
You can now write clear, searchable product listings that tell the truth.

check.q: What should you give AI when you ask it to draft a listing?
options: Only the product's real facts, and ask it to use only those
A competitor's listing to copy word for word
Nothing, so it can be creative
Claims you hope are true
check.why: AI drafts honest listings only when it works from your real facts.

check.q: AI's draft says your mug is "dishwasher safe", but you never tested it. What would you do?
options: Keep it because buyers like it
Add "probably" in front of it
Move it to the end of the description
Remove the claim until you can back it up
check.why: Product claims must be true and backed by evidence before you use them.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Making clean product images
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create product photos and graphics that show the real product clearly.
This lesson builds toward: Using a phone camera and an AI editing tool, you will create product images that show the real product clearly, with a size photo and no edit that changes how the product looks.
Photos sell products. Use your phone in daylight near a window, on a plain background, and take several angles plus a close-up and a photo showing size (in a hand or next to a common object).
AI tools can help: removing or changing backgrounds, fixing lighting, resizing for each platform, and making lifestyle graphics in tools like Canva. Many marketplaces have rules for the main image, such as a plain background; check the platform's image rules.
Never use AI to make the product look different from what the buyer will get: no fake colors, sizes, features or results. Misleading images can lead to returns, bad reviews, platform penalties and deceptive-advertising problems.
Step by step:
- Shoot in daylight on a plain background.
- Take several angles, a close-up and a size photo.
- Use AI tools to clean backgrounds and resize.
- Check the platform's image rules.
- Compare every image with the real product.
Words to know:
- Lifestyle image: a photo or graphic showing the product being used.
- Background removal: an editing tool that cuts the product out of its background.
Try it now: Photograph one product (angles, close-up, size), clean up the main image with an AI background tool, and compare it with the real product before using it.
You can now create clean, honest product images with AI editing help.

check.q: Which set of photos shows a product honestly and clearly?
options: One dark photo taken at night
A few angles, a close-up and a size photo
A single AI-made picture of a similar product
A photo with a busy background full of other items
check.why: Several angles, a close-up and a size photo show buyers what they will really get.

check.q: An AI tool made the color of your scarf brighter than it really is. What would you do?
options: Use it because it looks better
Use it but add a filter to the others too
Fix it so the image matches the real product
Delete all your photos and use stock images
check.why: Images must match the real product, or buyers will be misled and ask for refunds.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Shipping and returns policies
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write shipping and returns policies that follow the FTC's mail order rule.
This lesson builds toward: Using the FTC mail order rule, you will write shipping and returns policies and a delay message, with shipping times you can really meet and a refund offer in the delay message.
The FTC's Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule says: if you state a shipping time, you need a reasonable basis to believe you can meet it; if you do not state one, you must have a reasonable basis to ship within 30 days.
If you cannot ship on time, you must tell the buyer, give a revised date, and offer the choice to cancel for a prompt refund. Refunds for cash, check, money order or third-party credit cards must be made within seven working days after cancellation, and store credit cannot replace a required refund.
AI can draft clear policy pages: "Write a friendly shipping and returns policy for a small online shop. We ship in 3 to 5 business days. Returns accepted within 30 days for unused items; buyer pays return shipping." Then check it matches what you really do, and the platform's rules.
Step by step:
- Decide a shipping time you can really meet.
- Decide your returns rules.
- Ask AI to draft both policies in plain words.
- Check them against the FTC rule and your platform's rules.
- Write a delay message template that offers cancel-and-refund.
Words to know:
- Mail order rule: the FTC rule on shipping times, delay notices and refunds for orders by mail, internet or phone.
- Revised date: a new shipping date you give a buyer after a delay.
Official sources:
- FTC: Business Guide to the Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule
Try it now: Write your shipping and returns policies with AI, check them against the FTC rule, and write a delay message that gives a revised date and offers cancellation with a refund.
You can now set shipping and returns policies that are clear, honest and follow the FTC rule.

check.q: What should a shipping policy promise?
options: The fastest time any seller offers
No time at all, so you are never late
Next-day delivery for every order
A shipping time you have a real basis to meet
check.why: The FTC rule says you need a reasonable basis to meet any shipping time you state.

check.q: A supplier delay means an order will ship late. What would you do?
options: Tell the buyer, give a new date and offer to cancel with a refund
Say nothing and hope they do not notice
Offer only store credit
Cancel the order without telling them
check.why: The rule requires a delay notice with a revised date and the choice to cancel for a refund.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Answering customers with AI help
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create reply templates for the five questions your customers ask most.
This lesson builds toward: Given your shop's most common customer questions, you will create reply templates with AI help that use only your real policies, with five checked templates and no customer private details shared with the AI.
Online shops get the same questions again and again: Where is my order? Can I return this? What size should I get? Do you ship to my area? Is this in stock? Write templates for each, with blanks for details.
AI can draft friendly templates from your real policies. For new questions, summarize the question without the customer's name, address or order number and ask AI for a reply, then fill in details yourself.
If you add a chatbot to your store, give it only your real policies and product facts, tell customers it is automated, and make it easy to reach a person. Check what the chatbot service does with customer data.
Step by step:
- List the five questions customers ask most.
- Give AI your real policies and ask for templates with [blanks].
- Check each template against your policies.
- For new questions, summarize without private details.
- If using a chatbot, give it real facts and a route to a person.
Words to know:
- Reply template: a ready-made answer with blanks you fill in.
- Chatbot: an automated program that answers customer messages.
Try it now: Write five reply templates for your most common customer questions with AI, using only your real policies, and check each one.
You can now answer customer questions quickly and accurately with AI-drafted templates.

check.q: What makes a customer reply template safe to use?
options: It sounds friendly, even if facts are guessed
It is based on your real policies and checked by you
AI wrote it, so it must be right
It promises whatever the customer wants
check.why: Templates must match your real policies, so you check every one AI drafts.

check.q: A customer email includes their order number and home address. How would you get AI help with the reply?
options: Paste the whole email into the AI
Ask the customer to send the address again
Summarize the question without the private details
Post it in a public forum for advice
check.why: Leaving out private details protects the customer while still getting AI help.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Follow-up emails and reviews, the legal way
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a follow-up email and a review request that follow CAN-SPAM and the FTC review rules.
This lesson builds toward: Using CAN-SPAM and the FTC review rules, you will write a follow-up email and a review request, with an address, an opt-out and no fake or paid-for reviews.
Email to past buyers (thank-yous, restock news, offers) brings repeat sales. Use AI to draft short emails, and follow CAN-SPAM: honest From and subject lines, make clear it is an ad when it is, include your physical address and a clear opt-out, and honor opt-outs within 10 business days. Most store and email platforms add unsubscribe links for you.
Reviews build trust. Ask every buyer for an honest review, not only happy ones. The FTC's rule bans fake reviews and testimonials (including AI-generated ones from people who do not exist) and bans rewards given only for positive reviews. Never buy reviews or use AI to write them.
Use AI to read your reviews for patterns: what buyers love and what they complain about. Fix the top complaint, and mention the fix in your listings or emails.
Step by step:
- Draft a short follow-up email to past buyers with AI.
- Check it for CAN-SPAM basics: honest lines, address, opt-out.
- Draft an honest review request for every buyer.
- Never reward only good reviews or write reviews with AI.
- Use AI to find patterns in your real reviews.
Words to know:
- Repeat sale: a sale to someone who has bought before.
- Opt-out: a way to stop getting emails; unsubscribe.
Official sources:
- FTC: CAN-SPAM Act Compliance Guide for Business
- FTC: Final rule banning fake reviews and testimonials (press release)
Try it now: Final task: write one follow-up email and one review request that follow the rules, then assemble your launch kit: niche summary, three listings with images, policies, five reply templates, email and review request.
You can now run an online shop with AI help that is honest with buyers and follows US rules.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Niche with evidence The niche is a guess, or the only evidence is what AI said. The summary names the niche and gives real marketplace evidence of demand. It also names a problem from competitors' reviews that your product could fix. Honest listings A listing has a claim that is untrue or not checked. Three listings with a clear title, description and key details, all true. Each listing also uses the words buyers search for and answers size, materials and shipping time. Clear, real images Images are unclear, or an edit changes how the product looks. Each product has a clean main image and a size photo that match the real product. Each product also has several angles and a close-up of the details. Shipping and returns No shipping time, or a time you cannot meet; no delay plan. Written policies with a shipping time you can meet and a delay message that offers a refund. The returns policy also says clearly who pays return shipping and how fast refunds are sent. Customer replies Fewer than five templates, or a template that does not match your policies. Five checked templates based on your real policies. Templates also say when the customer will hear back and how to reach a person. Email and review request The email has no address or opt-out, or the review request offers a reward for good reviews. The email has your address and an opt-out, and the review request asks for honest reviews. The review request goes to every buyer, not only happy ones. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What must a marketing email to customers include?
options: A discount code
Your physical address and a way to opt out
A photo of every product
The customer's order history
check.why: CAN-SPAM requires a physical address and a working opt-out in marketing emails.

check.q: A friend offers to write five-star reviews for your shop. What would you do?
options: Accept, since they mean well
Accept only three of them
Ask AI to write a few more like them
Say no and ask real buyers for honest reviews
check.why: The FTC bans fake reviews, so you ask real buyers for honest ones.
